title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
description: The supreme masterpiece of the Alliterative Revival and one of the greatest poems of the English Middle Ages: 2,530 lines in alliterative stanzas with the 'bob and wheel' close, recounting Gawain's beheading-game with the Green Knight and his testing in the castle of Sir Bertilak. A romance of courtesy, chastity, and shame, in which the pentangle and the green girdle measure the hero against an ideal he cannot perfectly keep.
plot_or_argument: At Arthur's Christmas court, the Green Knight offers his axe-blow for a return stroke a year hence; Gawain beheads him, and the knight rides off alive. The following winter Gawain journeys to the Green Chapel, is entertained for three days at Hautdesert — where his host's wife tests his chastity with escalating temptations while the host hunts deer, boar, and fox in parallel scenes — and, having accepted the protective green girdle and concealed it, receives at the Chapel a nick on the neck: the girdle's shame is revealed as the whole adventure was Bertilak's design, set on him by Morgan le Fay.
narrative_structure: A two-part structure (the beheading game at Camelot; the journey, temptations, and exchange of winnings at Hautdesert), interlaced by the three parallel hunts and the three bedroom temptations, and closed by Gawain's return and Arthur's court's adoption of the girdle.
principal_characters: Gawain; the Green Knight (Sir Bertilak); Lady Bertilak; Arthur; Guinevere; Morgan le Fay; the guide
meter_and_prosody: The unrhymed alliterative long line in stanzas of varying length, each closed by the five-line rhymed 'bob and wheel'.
historical_context: Composed c. 1375–1400 by an unknown north-west Midlands poet (the 'Gawain-poet'), probably in the household circle of the Cheshire/Staffordshire gentry; preserved uniquely in BL Cotton MS Nero A.x, with Pearl, Patience, and Cleanness.
literary_significance: The most admired English romance ever written: its fusion of alliterative craft, courtly ideals, and moral seriousness — and its unmatched winter landscapes and temptation scenes — have made it a touchstone of English literature (translated by Tolkien, Armitage, and many others).
attribution_notes: Anonymous; attributed with Pearl, Patience, and Cleanness to the single 'Gawain-poet' on grounds of style, dialect, and shared manuscript.
bibliographical_notes: BL Cotton MS Nero A.x. Standard editions: J. R. R. Tolkien and E. V. Gordon, 2nd edn rev. N. Davis (1967); A Book of Middle English; M. Borroff (trans.).

title: Pearl
description: The great elegiac dream vision of the Gawain-poet: 1,212 lines in 101 twelve-line stanzas linked by concatenation, in which a grieving father, mourning a lost 'pearl' (his infant daughter), dreams of her transfigured among the blessed, debates with her the theology of grace, and glimpses the heavenly Jerusalem. The most perfectly wrought poem of the Alliterative Revival.
plot_or_argument: In an arbour where his pearl slipped from his hand, the dreamer falls asleep and finds himself by a crystal stream; across it stands a maiden crowned with pearls, whom he recognizes as his lost child grown in heaven. Their dialogue unfolds the parable of the vineyard — the justice of the penny's wage, the grace that admits the innocent and the repentant alike — and culminates in his vision of the New Jerusalem and the Lamb, before his waking returns him to the earth where the pearl is buried.
narrative_structure: Twenty sections of five stanzas each, the last line of each stanza echoed by the first of the next, and the poem's final line repeating its first; the stream divides the poem into the two worlds of earth and heaven.
principal_characters: the Dreamer (father); the Pearl-maiden; the Lamb; St John
meter_and_prosody: Twelve-line alliterative stanzas rhyming ababababbcbc, with concatenatio linking stanza to stanza.
historical_context: Composed c. 1375–1400 by the Gawain-poet in the north-west Midlands, in the Ricardian flowering of the dream vision; preserved uniquely in Cotton Nero A.x with Sir Gawain, Patience, and Cleanness.
literary_significance: The greatest English religious elegy and the most technically brilliant poem of the Middle English period; its theology of grace and its jewelled art have made it the centre of a vast critical literature.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; assigned to the Gawain-poet on grounds of style and shared manuscript.
bibliographical_notes: BL Cotton MS Nero A.x. Standard editions: E. V. Gordon (1953); A Book of Middle English; M. Andrew and R. Waldron, The Poems of the Pearl Manuscript, 5th edn (2007).

title: Patience
description: The Gawain-poet's homiletic poem of 531 lines on the prophet Jonah, expounding the beatitude 'blessed are the patient' through the comic drama of the reluctant prophet, the storm, the whale, and the withered woodbine. Patience, the poem argues, is the virtue God himself practises with sinners — and the one Jonah must learn.
plot_or_argument: Jonah, fleeing God's command to preach at Nineveh, boards ship for Tarshish; the storm God raises forces the sailors to cast him overboard, and he is swallowed by the whale, in whose belly he prays his psalm of thanksgiving; delivered, he preaches at Nineveh, whose repentance God accepts — to Jonah's fury, which the parable of the woodbine answers: if Jonah pities a plant, shall not God pity a city of a hundred and twenty thousand?
narrative_structure: A homiletic prologue on the eight beatitudes, then a three-movement biblical narrative (flight and storm; whale and prayer; Nineveh and the woodbine), with the parable as the poem's doctrinal climax.
principal_characters: Jonah; God; the sailors; the Ninevites
meter_and_prosody: The unrhymed alliterative long line, handled with colloquial vigour.
historical_context: Composed c. 1375–1400 by the Gawain-poet; preserved uniquely in Cotton Nero A.x. The Jonah story had a special medieval resonance through its typological link to the Resurrection.
literary_significance: The liveliest biblical poem of the alliterative revival and the most sustained Middle English treatment of patience; its comic sympathy with the reluctant prophet is without parallel in the period.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; assigned to the Gawain-poet on grounds of style and shared manuscript.
bibliographical_notes: BL Cotton MS Nero A.x. Standard editions: A Book of Middle English; Andrew and Waldron (2007).

title: Cleanness
description: The Gawain-poet's homiletic poem of 1,812 alliterative lines on purity ('clannesse'): expanding the gospel parable of the wedding feast, it retells the Flood, the destruction of Sodom, and Belshazzar's feast as three great exemplary narratives of God's vengeance on filth and pride, culminating in the writing on the wall. The most rhetorically powerful of the Cotton Nero poems.
plot_or_argument: From the parable of the guest without a wedding garment, the poet unfolds the doctrine of the clean heart; Noah's Flood shows God's cleansing of the world's filth; the destruction of Sodom his vengeance on unnatural lust; and Belshazzar's feast — with its vessels stolen from the Temple, its drunken blasphemy, and the mysterious hand writing Mene, Tekel, Peres — his judgement on sacrilege and pride.
narrative_structure: A homiletic frame (the beatitude 'blessed are the clean of heart' and the wedding parable) enclosing three parallel biblical exempla of increasing elaboration, each a set-piece of alliterative description.
principal_characters: Noah; Abraham; Lot; Belshazzar; Daniel; the Queen; God
meter_and_prosody: The unrhymed alliterative long line at its most sumptuous, with elaborate descriptive passages (the Flood, the feast, the Temple vessels).
historical_context: Composed c. 1375–1400 by the Gawain-poet; preserved uniquely in Cotton Nero A.x. The poem's courtly castigation of 'fylþe of þe flesch' speaks to the Ricardian culture of courtly and clerical reform.
literary_significance: The most powerful homiletic poem of the alliterative revival; its Belshazzar episode is among the greatest descriptive set-pieces in Middle English poetry.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; assigned to the Gawain-poet on grounds of style and shared manuscript.
bibliographical_notes: BL Cotton MS Nero A.x. Standard editions: A Book of Middle English; Andrew and Waldron (2007).

title: St Erkenwald
description: An alliterative miracle-legend of 352 lines on the discovery, during the rebuilding of St Paul's, of a pagan judge's incorrupt tomb: the bishop Erkenwald's tearful prayer draws from the corpse the story of his just life and the baptism that, in the moment of his speech, admits the just pagan to heaven. The finest short alliterative poem of the period.
plot_or_argument: Workmen excavating at St Paul's find a tomb whose body lies uncorrupted as in life; none can identify it, until Bishop Erkenwald, summoned to the mystery, speaks to the dead man, who reveals himself as a judge of heathen London, just in all his dealings; at the bishop's words of baptism, the corpse — denied heaven's sight so long — sighs, and crumbles to dust as its soul ascends.
narrative_structure: A single dramatic episode: discovery, wonder, dialogue, and resolution, in the manner of the alliterative miracle-legend.
principal_characters: Erkenwald; the pagan judge; the London crowd
meter_and_prosody: The unrhymed alliterative long line, restrained and solemn.
historical_context: Composed c. 1386–1400 in the north-west Midlands, in the circle of the Gawain-poet (many scholars assign it to him), perhaps occasioned by work on St Paul's; preserved uniquely in BL Harley MS 2250 (dated 1477).
literary_significance: The classic Middle English treatment of the salvation of the just pagan (the problem Dante faced with Trajan and Virgil), and one of the most moving poems of the alliterative tradition.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; attributed by many scholars to the Gawain-poet.
bibliographical_notes: BL Harley MS 2250. Standard editions: C. Peterson (1977); in Andrew and Waldron, The Poems of the Pearl Manuscript.

title: Piers Plowman
description: William Langland's visionary masterpiece, surviving in three authorial versions (the A-text c. 1367–70, B-text c. 1377–79, C-text c. 1386–88): a sequence of ten dream visions in which the dreamer Will searches for Truth, Dowel, Dobet, and Dobest through the estates of fourteenth-century England — the fair field full of folk, the pilgrimage of the seven deadly sins, the Tree of Charity, and the harrowing of hell. The greatest English poem of social and spiritual reform.
plot_or_argument: Will falls asleep on the Malvern Hills and sees a field full of folk between the Tower of Truth and the Dungeon of Wrong; the quest for St Truth becomes the ploughing of the half-acre under Piers the Plowman; the later visions pursue Dowel, Dobet, and Dobest through the confession of the sins, the feast of Patience, the Tree of Charity, the Passion and harrowing of hell, and the founding of Holy Church, which the final vision shows besieged from within by Antichrist and the friars.
narrative_structure: A series of ten (or eight) dream visions within dreams, progressing from social satire through theological allegory to apocalyptic vision, with Will's own spiritual biography as the connective thread; the B-text adds the great inner dreams of the C-text's revisions.
principal_characters: Will (the dreamer); Piers the Plowman; Holy Church; Lady Meed; Conscience; Patience; the Seven Deadly Sins; the Samaritan; Christ; Antichrist
literary_form: allegorical dream vision in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: The unrhymed alliterative long line, ranging from colloquial satire to liturgical sublimity.
historical_context: Composed and revised c. 1367–88, probably in London, against the background of plague, labour legislation, the Peasants' Revolt (1381), and Wycliffite controversy — all refracted in the poem's satire; preserved in over fifty manuscripts, more than any English poem except the Prick of Conscience.
literary_significance: With the Canterbury Tales and Sir Gawain, one of the three summits of Ricardian literature: its blend of estates satire, theological vision, and vernacular prophecy made it the rallying text of reform for two centuries, from the rebels of 1381 to the Tudor reformers who printed it.
attribution_notes: Attributed to William Langland by manuscript evidence and internal acrostic signatures; the three texts represent the author's own revisions.
bibliographical_notes: Over fifty manuscripts. Standard editions: A. V. C. Schmidt (B-text, 1978; rev. 2011); G. Kane and E. T. Donaldson (B-text, 1975); D. Pearsall (C-text, 1978).

title: Winner and Waster
description: The earliest datable poem of the Alliterative Revival (c. 1352): a debate dream vision in which Winner (the thrifty, hoarding merchant) and Waster (the lavish, spending lord) plead their cases before the king, who assigns each his proper sphere. Its satire of Edward III's economic policies — and its superb description of the armies — make it a key document of mid-century social thought.
plot_or_argument: The dreamer sees two armies drawn up in a land divided between wealth and want; Winner and Waster, their champions, dispute before the king: Winner attacks Waster's reckless feasting and ruinous retinues, Waster defends liberality as the lifeblood of the realm; the king's judgement — sending Winner to the papal court and the friars, Waster to London and the magnates — restores each to his proper economy.
narrative_structure: A debate vision framed by the arming of the two hosts, in the tradition of the altercatio; the poem breaks off, unfinished, in the king's judgement.
principal_characters: the Dreamer; Winner; Waster; the king (Edward III)
meter_and_prosody: The unrhymed alliterative long line, early and vigorous.
historical_context: Composed c. 1352, referencing the Order of the Garter (1348), the Statute of Treasons (1352), and the king's household; preserved uniquely in BL Additional MS 31042 (mid-fifteenth century), with a line lost to damage.
literary_significance: The earliest witness to the alliterative revival's social satire and the direct ancestor of Piers Plowman's field of folk; its economic debate has made it a touchstone for medieval political thought.
bibliographical_notes: BL Additional MS 31042. Standard edition: S. Trigg (1990); in A Book of Middle English.

title: The Parliament of the Three Ages
alternative_titles: The Parlement of the Thre Ages
description: An alliterative debate vision of the three ages of man: a dreamer watching a deer hunt overhears Youth, Middle Age, and Old Age dispute the values of their lives, in a poem that grafts the morality of the ages onto the romance glamour of the hunt and the nine worthies. Its hunt scene is among the finest descriptive passages of the revival.
plot_or_argument: The dreamer, concealed in the woods, follows the elaborate ritual of the hunt — the harbouring, the chase, the breaking of the deer — and then overhears three debaters: Youth, vaunting love and tournament; Middle Age, priding himself on wealth; and Old Age, who answers with the ubi sunt catalogue of the nine worthies and the lesson of Death the leveller.
narrative_structure: A frame vision enclosing the hunt and the three speeches, in the debate-vision convention.
principal_characters: the Dreamer; Youth; Middle Age; Old Age; Death
meter_and_prosody: The unrhymed alliterative long line with stanzaic variation.
historical_context: Composed c. 1370–90 in the north or north-west Midlands, drawing on the tradition of the ages of man and the nine worthies; preserved uniquely in BL Additional MS 31042 and (in part) Additional MS 33942.
literary_significance: The most accomplished of the alliterative debate visions after Winner and Waster, and a principal vernacular statement of the ages-of-man topos.
bibliographical_notes: BL Additional MSS 31042, 33942. Standard edition: M. Y. Offord, EETS OS 246 (1959).

title: Alliterative Morte Arthure
description: The great alliterative tragedy of King Arthur: some 4,300 lines recounting Arthur's continental conquests, his war against the emperor Lucius, and his fall through Mordred's treason and his own pride, culminating in his dream of Fortune's wheel and his death. A poem of imperial ambition and Christian judgement, preserved in the Thornton manuscript, and a principal source of Malory's Morte Darthur.
plot_or_argument: Arthur, refusing tribute to Rome, leads his army across the Channel, defeats the giant of Mont St Michel, and conquers the emperor Lucius; at the height of his power the dream of Fortune's wheel warns him of the fall to come, and the news of Mordred's rebellion and Guinevere's adultery brings him home to the final battle, where Gawain dies and Arthur, mortally wounded, is buried at Glastonbury.
narrative_structure: A two-movement tragedy of rise and fall, with the dream of Fortune as its pivot and the battles as its set-pieces.
principal_characters: Arthur; Gawain; Mordred; Guinevere; Lucius; the giant of Mont St Michel; Fortune
meter_and_prosody: The unrhymed alliterative long line at its most heroic, with formulaic battle diction.
historical_context: Composed c. 1400 in the north of England, blending chronicle history with romance matter and the tragedy of Fortune; preserved in the Thornton manuscript (Lincoln Cathedral MS 91, c. 1440) and used by Malory in his tale of Arthur and Lucius.
literary_significance: The most powerful Arthurian poem of the alliterative tradition and the classic English statement of Arthur's tragedy; its influence on Malory and on the modern Arthurian revival (Tennyson read it in Malory's shadow) is profound.
bibliographical_notes: Lincoln Cathedral MS 91 (Thornton). Standard editions: V. Krishna (1976); L. D. Benson, in King Arthur's Death (1974; rev. 1986).

title: The Destruction of Troy
alternative_titles: The Gest Hystoriale of the Destruction of Troy
description: The longest alliterative poem of the revival (over 14,000 lines), translating Guido delle Colonne's Latin Historia destructionis Troiae: the full Trojan story from Jason and the golden fleece to the fall of the city and the homecomings of the Greeks. A work of encyclopedic narrative scope, prized for its battles, storms, and sieges, preserved in a single manuscript.
plot_or_argument: The poem recounts the causes and course of the Trojan war — the Argonauts, the first destruction of Troy, the judgement of Paris and rape of Helen, the ten years' siege with its councils, battles, and single combats, the treachery of the wooden horse, the burning of the city, and the fates of the returning heroes.
narrative_structure: A continuous chronicle-romance in the Guido tradition, organized by the war's causes, course, and aftermath, with elaborate set-piece descriptions.
principal_characters: Hector; Achilles; Priam; Paris; Helen; Agamemnon; Ulysses; Troilus
meter_and_prosody: The unrhymed alliterative long line sustained over an unprecedented length.
historical_context: Composed c. 1385–1400 in the north-west Midlands, translating Guido delle Colonne (1287) with additions; preserved uniquely in Glasgow, Hunterian MS V.2.8 (mid-sixteenth century).
literary_significance: The fullest Middle English Troy narrative and the summit of alliterative translation; its matter links the revival to Lydgate's Troy Book and the Tudor Troy tradition.
bibliographical_notes: Hunterian MS V.2.8. Standard edition: H. Matsumoto (2011).

title: Piers the Plowman's Creed
description: A Lollard-leaning alliterative satire of some 850 lines in imitation of Piers Plowman: a simple man, seeking to learn his creed, questions the four orders of friars in turn and finds only greed, sophistry, and pride — until the ploughman Piers teaches him the creed in the plain words of charity and labour. The fiercest of the Piers Plowman imitations.
plot_or_argument: The narrator, who cannot say his creed, applies to the friars; each order's answer is a satiric portrait — their fine houses, their begging, their hatred of the ploughman's tithes — until Piers and his family, labouring in poverty, recite the creed and denounce the friars with apocalyptic anger.
narrative_structure: A quest-satire in the Piers tradition: four failed consultations with the friars, resolved by the ploughman's plain teaching.
principal_characters: the narrator; the four friars; Piers the Plowman; his wife and children
meter_and_prosody: The unrhymed alliterative long line with rhyme incorporated in places.
historical_context: Composed c. 1395 in the orbit of the Lollard movement, satirizing the friars' wealth in the spirit of FitzRalph and Wyclif; preserved in BL Royal MS 18 B.xvii and printed by the Tudor reformers (1553).
literary_significance: The most important literary offspring of Piers Plowman and the principal verse monument of Lollard satire; its Tudor printing made 'Piers Plowman' a name for English reform.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; formerly attributed to the author of the Plowman's Tale.
bibliographical_notes: BL Royal MS 18 B.xvii. Standard edition: J. Dean, TEAMS (2000).

title: The Awntyrs off Arthure
alternative_titles: The Anturs of Arther at the Tarnewathelan
description: An alliterative Arthurian poem of some 700 lines in two adventures: the ghost of Guinevere's mother, risen from a lake in Tarn Wadling to warn of pride and the fall of the Round Table, and the duel in which Gawain and Galeron contest disputed lands before Arthur's judgement. Its spectral first episode is among the most powerful scenes in the alliterative corpus.
plot_or_argument: While hunting at Tarn Wadling, Guinevere and Gawain meet a ghost who prophesies the ruin of Arthur's court and shows the torments of the dead; in the second adventure, Gawain fights the knight Galeron for the lands Arthur has granted him, and Arthur's equitable judgement restores them — with the ghost's warning shadowing the court's splendour.
narrative_structure: A two-part romance (ghostly warning; judicial combat) linked by the theme of land, justice, and mortality.
principal_characters: Gawain; Guinevere; the ghost of Guinevere's mother; Galeron; Arthur
meter_and_prosody: Thirteen-line alliterative stanzas with rhyme and wheel.
historical_context: Composed c. 1400 in the north of England, perhaps for a northern gentry audience with an interest in its Cumberland setting; preserved in four manuscripts and printed in the sixteenth century.
literary_significance: The finest of the northern Gawain romances after Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, and the classic statement of the ghost-warning topos in Arthurian verse.
bibliographical_notes: Lincoln Cathedral MS 91 (Thornton); Douce MS 324; etc. Standard edition: in Sir Gawain: Eleven Romances and Tales, TEAMS (1995).

title: The Siege of Jerusalem
description: An alliterative poem of some 1,300 lines on the Roman destruction of Jerusalem by Vespasian and Titus, cast as vengeance for the crucifixion: the siege, the famine, the fall of the city, and the punishment of the Jews who bought and tortured Christ. A poem of notorious violence whose anti-Judaism reflects the worst of its age, and a major witness to the romance of Christian vengeance.
plot_or_argument: Titus, healed by the vernicle, vows vengeance on the Jews; the poem narrates the siege and its horrors — the famine, the mother who eats her child, the crucifixions and selling of Jews — and the city's destruction, framed throughout as the working out of Christ's blood-debt.
narrative_structure: A single-movement siege narrative built from the French Vengeance tradition, with the torments of the Jews as its repeated set-pieces.
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative long lines in couplets and stanzaic clusters.
historical_context: Composed c. 1390 in the north-west Midlands, from the French Vengeance de Nostre Seigneur and related sources; preserved in nine manuscripts, including the Thornton manuscript and Bodleian Laud Misc. 656.
literary_significance: The most widely copied alliterative poem of its theme and a text of central importance — and difficulty — for the study of medieval Christian anti-Judaism in literature.
bibliographical_notes: Nine manuscripts, incl. Bodleian Laud Misc. 656. Standard edition: R. Hanna and D. Lawton, EETS OS 320 (2003).

title: The Buke of the Howlat
description: Richard Holland's Scottish alliterative beast-allegory of some 1,000 lines, composed c. 1448 for the Douglas family: the owl, ashamed of his ugliness, appeals through the assembly of birds to the pope and the emperor, each bird vying in flattery, until Dame Nature restores him to his proper worth. A satire of pride, courts, and flattery, and the last major alliterative poem of the tradition.
plot_or_argument: The howlat, complaining of his feathers, is counselled by the peacock to seek redress; the birds assemble in parliament before the pope and emperor, but the debate degenerates into mutual slander and sycophancy, until Nature intervenes, clothes the owl in dignity, and the poem ends with the Douglas heraldry and the family's praise.
narrative_structure: A beast-parliament in the Chaucerian manner, framed by the owl's complaint and closed by the heraldic celebration of the Douglases.
principal_characters: the Howlat; the Peacock; the Pope; the Emperor; Dame Nature; the birds of the parliament
meter_and_prosody: Thirteen-line alliterative stanzas with rhyme and wheel, in Older Scots.
historical_context: Composed c. 1448 by Richard Holland, secretary to Archibald Douglas, Earl of Moray, for the Douglas family at a moment of their power; preserved in the Asloan and Bannatyne manuscripts (c. 1515, 1568).
literary_significance: The last major alliterative poem in the British tradition and a key document of Douglas politics, heraldry, and the Scottish reception of the Alliterative Revival.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Richard Holland on the evidence of the poem's colophon and Douglas records.
bibliographical_notes: National Library of Scotland, Asloan MS; Bannatyne MS. Standard edition: R. Hanna, STS (2014).
